Thank you for submitting your article "Threat prediction as the relevant factor for understanding fear generalization" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by Richard Ivry as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

This study uses eye movements collected from a large sample of human subjects (N=74) to test whether generalization of learned fear responses is driven by unspecific perceptual similarity or by perceptual similarity exclusively along dimensions that are relevant for distinguishing the CS+ from the CS-. The experimental design used 8 face stimuli which varied along two dimensions (gender and identity), spanning a circle. Subjects first viewed all 8 faces in a baseline session and then two faces (180 degree apart, thus varying only on one dimension) were associated with shock (CS+) and no-shock (CS-) in a conditioning session. Finally, subjects viewed all stimuli again in a generalization session. Fixation patterns in the baseline session were well predicted by a model of the circular organization of the stimulus set. However, pre-post conditioning changes were best explained by a model that separated the relevant and irrelevant dimension, and showed that changes occurred exclusively along the relevant stimulus dimension. This shows that aversive learning leads to specific changes only along the relevant stimulus dimension.

Overall the reviewers felt that this is an interesting study that uses a sophisticated analysis to address an important question. However, reviewers also had major concerns about the framing of the paper, the data and conclusions. Perhaps the most critical is the focus on generalization with limited ability to really test the two models of generalization using the current design, and the lack of evidence for the reproducibility of the findings.

Essential revisions:

1) The reviewers agreed that there is an element of this study which is potentially informative for models of generalization, but that it doesn't reduce to the simple competing/alternative theories set out by the authors because the study design is not optimal to test the hypothesis as stated. However, there was broad consensus among reviewers that the strongest and most interesting part of this paper is that fear conditioning directs eye movements to features of faces that are most relevant for predicting whether a shock will occur. This is related to the concept of active sensing (i.e., information-seeking) and conditioning driving attentional resources in the domain of face processing. This was the focus of the 2017 biorxiv paper (doi: doi.org/10.1101/125682), which concluded: "These findings show that aversive learning can introduce substantial remodeling of exploration patterns in an adaptive manner during viewing of faces." This conclusion is much closer to and fully supported by the data. The reviewers would therefore encourage the authors to rewrite their manuscript (and change the title) such that it focuses on the core findings concerning the effect of conditioning on exploratory eye movements, and fully move potential implications for models of generalization to the Discussion.

2) With the new focus on the basic patterns of eye movements, it would be important to also include more descriptive data to show what features in the fixation patterns drive the dissimilarity between faces along the relevant and irrelevant dimension. For instance, fixation heatmaps, scan paths, saccade statistics, blink statistics, etc. might be useful.

3) Reviewers were concerned that the current design does not dissociate effects of fear conditioning from the effects of repeated exposure to the CS faces during conditioning. This could be ruled out by separately analyzing the first and second half of the generalization session, with the prediction that if the effects are driven by differential exposure, the effect of the unspecific component should increase over time (i.e., after subjects are also exposed to all other stimuli). In contrast, no changes in the unspecific component would suggest that the results are driven by aversive learning rather than exposure per se.

4) Although the study sample is large (N=74), there were concerns that because the results come from a complex analysis, they may not replicate out-of-sample. Ideally, the authors would collect new data and show that the effects replicate in an independent sample. Alternatively, they could use analytical approaches (k-fold cross-validation, etc.) to provide more evidence that the results are reliable and reproducible. In particular, it would be important to show that the pre-post conditioning difference in CS+ and in CS- gaze patterns, and their interaction, is robust and replicable.

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Fixation-Pattern Similarity Analysis Reveals Adaptive Changes in Face-Viewing Strategies Following Aversive Learning" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Richard Ivry as the Senior Editor, and three reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

Whereas reviewer 1 and 2 felt that the revised manuscript adequately addressed the initial concerns, reviewer 3 had some remaining comments. Based on our discussion, we ask:

1) The reviewers agreed that the manuscript would benefit from discussing two key limitations. These include an acknowledgement of the exploratory and relatively weak nature of the findings, and a discussion of possible disadvantages that come with the circular stimulus organization.

2) An additional concern regards the lack of an out-of-sample replication, which is compounded by the fact that only 65% of subjects behave according to the adversity gradient model. The reviewers are aware that collection of new data is not possible at this point. Instead, reviewer 3 recommends an additional analysis treating "model identity" as a random effect (e.g. using spm_BMS). In the event that the model comparison does not yield conclusive results, it should be discussed why this is the case. There are two possibilities why the group-level winning model only wins in 65% of the subjects. First, there is heterogeneity between subjects in the true mechanism. In this case, RFX is appropriate and should be used and reported. Or, the theoretical assumption is that they all use the same mechanism but data are too noisy for single-subject inference. It would be important if the authors could take a strong stance here (either model heterogeneity or noisy data), based on some theoretical considerations, and suggest appropriate future research steps to verify or falsify these conclusions.

results.result: Eight face stimuli were calibrated using a V1 model to form a circular similarity continuum with perfect circular organization in a two-dimensional perceptual space defined by gender and identity dimensions.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C13, C86, and C87 collectively describe the stimulus calibration procedure. The use of a V1 model (C86) and MDS analysis (C87) to achieve circular organization is methodologically sound and well-documented. The stress values reported (0.42, 0.04, 0.03 for 1D, 2D, 3D) support the two-dimensional organization.

results.result: Aversive conditioning successfully established differential responses to CS+ versus CS- faces, as evidenced by physiological (SCR 3.8x higher for CS+) and subjective measures (highest expectancy ratings for CS+), with Gaussian models fitting the data better than flat or binary models.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17 provide converging evidence from multiple measures (SCR, ratings) with appropriate statistical tests (paired t-tests, log-likelihood ratio tests, AIC comparisons). The model comparison at both group and individual levels (C17: 72/74 and 68/74 subjects for ratings, 58/63 for SCR) demonstrates robust conditioning effects.

results.result: Before aversive learning, exploration patterns exhibited a circular similarity structure that mirrored the physical similarity structure of the face stimuli, with the Perceptual Baseline Model significantly outperforming a null model.
results.evaluation: Claims C18, C23-C28, and C70 describe baseline exploration patterns with quantitative support (dissimilarity values 1.05±0.01 for neighbors vs 1.21±0.01 for opposing faces, t(73)=7.41, p<0.001). Model comparison statistics (BIC, adjusted r²=0.09, p<10⁻⁵) and significant parameter estimates (w_Circle=0.09±0.01, t(73)=7.99, p<0.001) provide strong evidence.

results.result: Aversive learning induced selective changes in exploration patterns along the adversity-specific dimension (CS+ to CS- axis) but not the orthogonal unspecific dimension, with the Adversity Gradient Model outperforming the simpler Perceptual Expansion Model.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C19, C32-C41, and C72 provide comprehensive statistical support including: specific dimension increase (1.21±0.02 to 1.27±0.02, t(73)=2.54, p<0.05) versus no change in orthogonal dimension (t(73)=-0.34, p=0.73), significant ANOVA interaction (F(1,73)=8.53, p<0.005), and superior model fit (BIC=-1957.5 vs -1697.4, adjusted r²=0.48 vs 0.35). The convergence of multiple statistical approaches strengthens this conclusion.

results.result: The anisotropy effect (increased dissimilarity along the specific dimension) was present in 65% of participants overall and 69% of successful learners, with Gaussian mixture modeling not supporting distinct subpopulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44 and C80 acknowledge individual variability while providing evidence against population heterogeneity. The Gaussian mixture model analysis (C44) appropriately tests for subpopulations and finds no support for multiple components, which is an important methodological strength addressing the moderate prevalence of the effect.

results.result: The CS+ Attraction Model, which included a Gaussian component centered on CS+, did not outperform the simpler Adversity Gradient Model, with parameter estimates for the CS+-centered component not significantly different from zero.
results.evaluation: Claims C45 and C46 provide model comparison evidence (BIC=-1957.5 vs -1923.6) and non-significant parameter estimates (baseline: t(73)=-0.27, p=0.78; generalization: t(73)=0.74, p=0.46). This appropriately rules out a CS+-specific attraction hypothesis through both model comparison and parameter testing.

results.result: Anisotropy in exploration patterns showed weak but significant correlation with subjective ratings of fear tuning (r=0.25, p=0.03) and marginal correlation with SCR (r=0.23, p=0.07).
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48 report weak correlations with one reaching significance and one marginal. While this suggests a relationship between exploration changes and aversive learning, the effect sizes are small (r~0.25) and one measure is only marginally significant. The correlations support but do not strongly establish the link between anisotropy and learning strength. Additional validation would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: The unspecific component did not increase with repeated exposure across generalization runs, suggesting that changes in exploration patterns were driven by affective learning rather than mere exposure.
results.evaluation: Claims C49, C82, and C83 address the alternative explanation of exposure effects. The run-by-run analysis showing no increase (and potential decrease) in the unspecific component provides evidence against exposure-driven effects. Combined with the correlation with learning measures (C47-C48), this supports the affective learning interpretation, though C83 appropriately frames this as the authors' belief rather than definitive proof.

results.result: Support vector machines could decode CS+ versus CS- trials with 56% accuracy in the generalization phase (versus 50% baseline), showing a significant interaction between phase and component, with within-subject but not across-subject training producing this effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C54 provide SVM classification results with appropriate statistics (ANOVA interaction F(72)=5.4, p=0.02; main effect F(73)=16.8, p=0.0001). The finding that across-subject training failed to reproduce the effect (F(73)=0.43, p=0.51) appropriately demonstrates idiosyncrasy in viewing patterns and validates the within-subject FPSA approach. The modest accuracy improvements (6% for specific, 2% for unspecific) are consistent with subtle effects.

results.result: Changes in exploration patterns following aversive learning were localized to the eye region of faces, as demonstrated by searchlight FPSA and ROI-based analyses showing significant anisotropy differences only in the eye region.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C55-C56, C59-C60 converge on eye region localization through multiple methods (SVM activation patterns, searchlight FPSA, ROI analysis). The ROI analysis shows significance only in the eye region (p<0.024, though uncorrected), and this occurred despite decreased fixation density in that region (C62), ruling out simple saliency explanations. The convergence of methods strengthens this conclusion.

results.result: Adversity-specific exploration emerged early, reaching significance at 400-900ms post-stimulus onset and starting after the first landing fixation, then remaining constant throughout stimulus presentation.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58 and C73 provide temporal characterization with statistical support (paired t-test, p=0.03 at 400-900ms window). The analysis using both time windows and fixation rank provides converging evidence for early onset. However, the temporal analysis was restricted to successful learners (n=61), which should be noted as a limitation.

results.result: The eye region accounted for ~72% of all fixations, with aversive learning causing a ~5% decrease in eye region fixations and corresponding increases in nose (+3.6%) and mouth (+0.6%) fixations.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 and C66-C68 provide quantitative descriptions of fixation distribution changes. These findings are important because they show that increased anisotropy in the eye region occurred despite decreased fixation density there, ruling out simple explanations based on increased attention to that region. The consistency with prior literature (C66 cites Walker-Smith et al., 1977) adds credibility.

results.result: Classical eye-movement features (fixation number, saccade distance, entropy) showed some differences between CS+ and CS-, but only saccade length exhibited significant generalization tuning, and none could predict FPSA anisotropy or showed fear-tuned fixation density in ROI analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65 and C69 demonstrate that traditional univariate measures were less sensitive than FPSA. The failure of classical features to predict anisotropy (F(4,69)=0.075, p=0.55, R²=-0.01) and the lack of significant tuning in ROI-based fixation counts (p>0.05 for all regions) justify the need for the multivariate FPSA approach. This strengthens the methodological contribution.

results.result: Eye-movement patterns show strong inter-individual variability (80% classification accuracy for subject identity), but FPSA overcomes this limitation by exploiting within-subject changes in similarity relationships and assessing all pairwise stimulus comparisons.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C78 provide methodological justification for FPSA. The high subject identification accuracy (C76, ~80%) demonstrates substantial idiosyncrasy, supporting the need for within-subject analyses. Claims C77-C78 explain how FPSA addresses this limitation, though these are primarily methodological explanations rather than empirical findings.

results.result: The selective changes in fixation strategies along the threat-predictive dimension support the threat-prediction model over the perceptual model of fear generalization, demonstrating that aversive learning affects the entire sensory-motor loop at the systems level.
results.evaluation: Claims C74 and C84 provide theoretical interpretation of the findings. The selective changes along the adversity-specific dimension (supported by C2, C19, C32-C41) provide evidence for threat-prediction over perceptual similarity models. However, these are interpretive claims that go beyond the direct data, and alternative explanations (addressed in C71, C83) should be considered.

results.result: The study included 74 participants (37 male, 37 female, age 27±4) who freely viewed eight faces before and after aversive conditioning, with high-quality eye-tracking (91% of runs with calibration ≤0.5°) and SCR data available for 63 participants.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C22, C85, C88-C90 provide methodological details about participants and data quality. The sample size (n=74) is adequate for the analyses performed, eye-tracking calibration quality is excellent (mean error 0.36°), and the loss of SCR data for 11 participants due to technical problems is transparently reported. The balanced gender composition is appropriate for face stimuli varying in gender.
